question: A 3-week-old neonate's chest radiograph shows a prominent triangular opacity projecting from the right side of the superior mediastinum, widening the upper mediastinum. The infant is feeding well and has no respiratory distress. What is the most likely explanation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Lymphoma is exceedingly rare in the neonatal period and this clinical picture does not fit. A well, feeding neonate with a triangular right-upper mediastinal opacity has a normal thymic sail sign until proven otherwise.

answers.text: The normal thymic sail sign — the infant thymus projects into the superior mediastinum and should not be mistaken for pathology.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The thymic sail sign is a classic normal variant in neonates and infants up to 2 years. The thymus is large relative to body size in early life and projects as a triangular or wavy opacity in the superior mediastinum. In a well, asymptomatic infant it is a normal finding and does not require investigation.

answers.text: Right upper lobe collapse requiring urgent physiotherapy.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Collapse produces a different pattern — volume loss with tracheal or mediastinal shift toward the collapsed side. A prominent triangular superior mediastinal opacity in a well neonate is characteristic of the normal thymic sail sign.

answers.text: Pleural effusion in the right thorax requiring drainage.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A pleural effusion would appear as a homogenous opacity at the lung base with blunting of the costophrenic angle, not as a superior mediastinal triangular opacity. This is the normal thymic sail sign.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the section on paediatric normal appearances. The thymic sail sign is one of the two most commonly misread normal variants in neonates and infants.
Correct. The thymic sail sign is a normal variant in neonates — the large thymus projects into the superior mediastinum.
